fields.title: The First Letter of John
fields.subtitle: Iōannou A, “First of John”
fields.description: A letter with no greeting and no farewell, written by an old pastor to his “dear children” after a painful split in their church, so that those who stayed might know they have eternal life. It opens with the life that was heard, seen and touched with human hands, and returns again and again to three tests: what we believe about Jesus, whether we keep his commands, and whether we love one another. God is light; God is love; love has no room for fear; and we love because he loved us first. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the First Letter of John?
qa.answer: The twenty-third book of the New Testament, the longest of three letters that bear John’s name. It has no greeting or farewell and reads like a pastor’s sermon to a church he knows well. Written after a group had left the church denying that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh, it gives the believers who stayed ways to recognise the truth and to be sure of their standing with God. It states its own purpose in 5:13: so that you may know that you have eternal life.

qa.question: Who wrote 1 John, and when was it written?
qa.answer: The letter does not name its author. He writes as an eyewitness of Jesus and as a father to his readers, in language very close to the Gospel of John. From the second century the church received it as the work of John the apostle, writing late in life at Ephesus, probably in the last decades of the first century. Some scholars think it came from a leader in the circle that treasured John’s witness, perhaps the “elder” of 2 and 3 John.

qa.question: Why was 1 John written?
qa.answer: A group had left the church (“They went out from among us”, 2:19). They denied that Jesus is the Christ and would not confess him as one who has come in the flesh, while claiming to know God. The letter does not name them, and scholars debate whether they held the views later taught by Cerinthus or by those who said Christ only seemed to have a body. The writer reassures those who stayed and gives them tests of true faith: right belief about Jesus, obedience to his commands, and love for one another.

qa.question: What does “God is love” mean in 1 John?
qa.answer: The phrase occurs twice, in 4:8 and 4:16, alongside the earlier statement that “God is light” (1:5). The letter says love is found first not in our love for God but in his love for us, shown in sending his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins (4:10). Because God is love, anyone who knows him will love others, not in words only but in deeds (3:18), and love leaves no room for fear (4:18).

qa.question: Does 1 John teach that Christians do not sin?
qa.answer: It says both that anyone who claims to be free from sin is fooling themselves (1:8) and that whoever is born of God “does not go on sinning” (3:9). The tense of the Greek in chapter 3 describes a settled way of life rather than every single act. John Wesley drew on these verses for his teaching on Christian perfection; others read them as describing the direction of a believer’s life. All agree the letter calls Christians to holiness and promises forgiveness to those who confess their sins (1:9; 2:1–2).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Like most modern Bibles it does not include the words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit found in 5:7 of the King James Version, which are not in any early Greek manuscript. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
God is love. Whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in them.

— 1 John 4:16

First John is called a letter, but it does not begin like one. There is no greeting, no name of the sender, no name of the church, no “grace and peace”. And it does not end like one either: no news, no list of friends, no farewell, only a single abrupt line, “Dear children, guard yourselves against idols.” What lies between reads less like correspondence than like a pastor speaking to a congregation he has known for years, whose names he no longer needs to say.

He calls them “dear children” again and again. Something has shaken them badly, and he writes to steady them: to tell them what is true, and how to know that they belong to it.

The vocabulary is as small as the Gospel of John’s, and many of the words are the same: light and darkness, truth and lies, life and death, love, remain, know, the world. The sentences are short and plain enough for a beginner in Greek to read. Yet few books of the Bible are harder to outline, because the writer does not move in a straight line. He circles. He takes up a theme, lays it down, and comes back to it a chapter later from another side, each time a little deeper. The repetitions are the point.

Something we touched with our hands

The opening is one long, breathless sentence that reaches across the first three verses:

What was there from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our own eyes, what we looked at closely and touched with our hands—this is what we are speaking about: the word of life. That life was revealed. We have seen it, and we testify to it, and we announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us. We announce to you as well what we have seen and heard, so that you too may have fellowship with us. The fellowship we share is with the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ.

— 1 John 1:1–3

Every reader of John’s Gospel will hear the echo. The Gospel begins “In the beginning was the Word”; the letter begins with “what was there from the beginning” and calls it “the word of life”. But the stress has moved. The Gospel announces that the Word became flesh; the letter insists, with three senses piled on one another, that this flesh was really there to be heard, seen and handled. That insistence is the first clue to why the letter was written.

Why it was written

The church the writer addresses has just been through a split:

They went out from among us, but they were never truly part of us. If they had been part of us, they would have remained with us. Their leaving happened so that it would be made plain that none of them are part of us.

— 1 John 2:19

The letter never names the people who left, and we cannot know exactly who they were. But it lets us see what they said and how they lived. They denied “that Jesus is the Christ” (2:22). They would not confess “Jesus Christ as one who has come in the flesh” (4:2). They claimed to know God and to be in the light, and to be free from sin, while caring little for keeping his commands or for the brothers and sisters they had left behind.

Many readers connect this with teachings known soon afterward. Some taught that the divine Christ only seemed to have a human body, and so could not truly have suffered; Ignatius of Antioch, writing to churches in the same region, argues against them hard. Others, like Cerinthus, whom Irenaeus says the apostle John met at Ephesus, taught that the heavenly Christ came upon the man Jesus at his baptism and left him before the cross. That may be why the letter speaks of Jesus Christ as “the one who came by water and blood” (5:6): not by the water of baptism only, but by the blood of his death as well. Whether the people who left held either view, scholars still debate. What is clear is that the dispute was over whether God had truly come among us in a human life and death, and that it left those who stayed wondering whether they were in the wrong.

So the writer says plainly why he wrote:

I have written these things to you so that you may know that you have eternal life—you who believe in the name of the Son of God.

— 1 John 5:13

It is worth setting that sentence beside the purpose of the Gospel, which was written “so that you may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name” (John 20:31). The Gospel was written so that its readers might come to believe. The letter was written to people who already believe, so that they might know.

The tests of life

How can they know? A Scottish scholar, Robert Law, called his study of this letter The Tests of Life, and the name has stuck. Three tests run through the book, woven together and returning again and again.

  • What you believe about Jesus. The true confession is that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, come in the flesh. “Anyone who denies the Son is without the Father as well; anyone who confesses the Son has the Father too” (2:23).
  • Whether you keep his commands. “We can be sure that we have come to know him in this way: if we keep his commands” (2:3). Anyone who claims to remain in him “ought to live in the same way that Jesus lived” (2:6).
  • Whether you love your brothers and sisters. “We know that we have moved out of death into life, because we love our brothers and sisters” (3:14).

The tests are not hurdles set up to keep people out. They are signs given to the anxious, so that they can stop wondering. Belief, obedience and love are not three different religions. They are one life, seen from three sides, and in 3:23 the writer ties them together in a single sentence: we are to believe in the name of God’s Son Jesus Christ, and to love one another.

God is light, God is love

Twice the letter says what God is, in three words each. The first comes near the start: “God is light, and in him there is no darkness, not the least” (1:5). The second comes near the end, and twice: “God is love” (4:8, 16). Together they carry the whole letter. Because God is light, no one can walk in darkness and claim to be with him. Because God is love, no one can hate a brother or sister and claim to know him.

And the letter is careful to say where love is found. It is not first our feeling toward God, but his action toward us:

This is where love is found: not in our having loved God, but in his loving us and sending his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins.

— 1 John 4:10

Love has a shape, and its shape is the cross: “This is how we have come to know what love is: he laid down his life for us” (3:16). Then, at once, the writer brings it down to the ground. If someone has enough of this world’s goods and shuts their heart against a brother or sister in need, “How can the love of God remain in such a person?” (3:17). Love that only talks is not love. “Dear children, let us love not by what we say or with our tongues, but by what we do and in truth” (3:18).

The puzzle of sin

Every careful reader of 1 John runs into the same puzzle. In the first chapter the writer says, “If we claim that we are free from sin, we are fooling ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1:8). In the third he says, “Whoever has been born of God does not go on sinning” (3:9). How can both be true?

Part of the answer is in the tense of the Greek verbs, which in chapter 3 describe a settled way of life, a person who keeps on sinning as a matter of course. The Christian is not sinless, but neither is sin any longer their home. Christians have weighed these verses differently. John Wesley found in them a promise that believers may be so filled with love as to be free from wilful sin, and drew heavily on this letter for his teaching on Christian perfection; others, in the Reformed tradition, have read them as describing the direction of a life rather than its every step. Both sides take seriously what the letter holds together: a high call to holiness, and a sure remedy when we fall short.

My dear children, I am writing this to you so that you will not sin. Yet if anyone does sin, we have an advocate in the Father’s presence, Jesus Christ, who is righteous. He himself is the sacrifice that atones for our sins, and not for ours alone but for the sins of the whole world.

— 1 John 2:1–2

The writer does not want his children to sin. But if they do, he does not want them to despair. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous: he will forgive our sins and cleanse us from every kind of wrongdoing” (1:9).

Remain

The word to watch in 1 John is remain, more than twenty times in five short chapters: God’s word remains in us, we remain in him and he in us. It is the word Jesus uses of the vine in John 15: “Remain in me, and I will remain in you.” The people who left did not remain. The letter’s whole appeal is that those who stayed should go on staying, because they have found where life is.

When our hearts condemn us

The letter’s tests could be turned into a weapon against the tender-hearted, who are always ready to fail themselves. The writer sees that danger and meets it in one of the kindest sentences in the New Testament:

This is how we will know that we belong to the truth, and how we will set our hearts at rest in his presence whenever our hearts condemn us: God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.

— 1 John 3:19–20

Assurance rests finally not on how we feel about ourselves but on God, who knows everything. “Love has no room for fear; instead, complete love throws fear out” (4:18).

Who wrote 1 John?

The letter, like the Gospel, never names its author. He writes as one of a group of eyewitnesses (“what we have seen with our own eyes”) and as a father to his readers. Its language and thought are so close to the Gospel of John that most readers, ancient and modern, have taken them to come from the same hand or the same circle. From the second century the church received it as the work of John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, writing late in life at Ephesus, probably in the last decades of the first century. Some scholars think it was written by a leader in the community that treasured John’s witness, perhaps the “elder” of 2 and 3 John, whom Eusebius, reading Papias, took to be a second John.

How to read 1 John

Read it aloud, at one sitting; it takes about twenty minutes. The prologue (1:1–4) announces the life that was seen and touched. Then the letter moves in widening circles: walking in the light (1:5–2:17); the antichrists and the anointing (2:18–27); children of God (2:28–3:24); testing the spirits and the love of God (4:1–21); and faith, testimony and assurance (5:1–21).

Notice the families of the letter: the “dear children”, and the fathers, young men and children of 2:12–14. Notice how often it says “we know”. Notice that its tests always come back to Jesus. And notice that its last word, about idols, is not an afterthought. A false picture of God is an idol, however spiritual it sounds. The letter has spent five chapters showing us the true one: “This one is the true God, and eternal life” (5:20).

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 1 John are worth knowing about before you begin.

“Remain.” Where older Bibles vary between “abide”, “continue” and “dwell”, this translation keeps “remain” throughout, so that a reader can follow one Greek word through the whole letter and back into John 15.

“Go on sinning.” In 3:6–9 and 5:18 the translation gives the force of the Greek tense: the one born of God “does not go on sinning”. It does not make the letter say that Christians never sin, which 1:8–10 denies.

“The sacrifice that atones for our sins.” In 2:2 and 4:10 a single Greek word, rendered in older Bibles “propitiation”, is translated by what it means: a sacrifice that deals with sin and turns away its judgment.

1 John 5:7–8. Readers of the King James Version will miss a line here: “the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one”. Those words are not found in any early Greek manuscript; they entered printed Greek New Testaments in the sixteenth century. This translation, like nearly every modern Bible, reads only “For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water and the blood, and the three are in agreement.”

“Brothers and sisters.” Where the Greek “brother” means any fellow believer, as it almost always does in this letter, the translation says “brother or sister”. The Open Word Bible also lets a reader choose “Christ” or “the Messiah” for Christos; this edition prints “Christ”.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 1 John 1
fields.body_html:
The life that was revealed

What was there from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our own eyes, what we looked at closely and touched with our hands—this is what we are speaking about: the word of life. That life was revealed. We have seen it, and we testify to it, and we announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us. We announce to you as well what we have seen and heard, so that you too may have fellowship with us. The fellowship we share is with the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ. We put these things in writing so that our joy may be complete.

Walking in the light

Now this is the message we heard from him and are declaring to you: God is light, and in him there is no darkness, not the least. If we claim to have fellowship with him while we go on walking in the darkness, we are lying and are not living by the truth. But if we walk in the light, just as he is in the light, we share fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son, goes on cleansing us from every sin. If we claim that we are free from sin, we are fooling ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous: he will forgive our sins and cleanse us from every kind of wrongdoing. If we claim that we have never sinned, we are calling him a liar, and his word is not in us.
fields.summary: John proclaims the word of life, which was revealed and which the apostles heard, saw and touched. God is light, and those who walk in the light have fellowship and are cleansed from sin, while those who confess their sins are forgiven.

fields.title: 1 John 2
fields.body_html:
Jesus, our advocate with the Father

My dear children, I am writing this to you so that you will not sin. Yet if anyone does sin, we have an advocate in the Father’s presence, Jesus Christ, who is righteous. He himself is the sacrifice that atones for our sins, and not for ours alone but for the sins of the whole world.

Knowing God and keeping his commands

We can be sure that we have come to know him in this way: if we keep his commands. Anyone who says, “I have come to know him,” but does not keep his commands is a liar, and the truth is not in them. But whoever keeps his word, in that person the love of God has truly reached its goal. That is how we know we are in him. Anyone who claims to remain in him ought to live in the same way that Jesus lived.

A command both old and new

Dear friends, what I am writing to you is not a new command but an old one, one you have had from the beginning. That old command is the word you heard. And yet the command I am writing to you is a new one. Its newness is real in him and in you, for the darkness is passing away, and already the true light is shining. Someone who says they are in the light, and yet hates their brother or sister, is in the darkness even now. Whoever loves their brother or sister remains in the light, and in them there is nothing that causes stumbling. But whoever hates their brother or sister is in the darkness and goes about in it, not knowing where they are headed, because the darkness has blinded their eyes.

Why I am writing to you

Dear children, I am writing to you because your sins stand forgiven for the sake of his name. Fathers, I am writing to you because you know the one who has been from the beginning. Young men, I am writing to you because you have defeated the evil one. Children, I have written to you because you know the Father. Fathers, I have written to you because you know the one who has been from the beginning. Young men, I have written to you because you are strong, God’s word remains in you, and you have defeated the evil one.

Do not love the world

Do not give your love to the world or to the things that are in it. Whoever loves the world has no love for the Father in them. For everything in the world—the cravings of human nature, the greed of the eyes, and arrogant pride in what one has—does not come from the Father but comes from the world. The world is passing away, and its cravings with it; but the one who does God’s will remains forever.

The last hour and the antichrists

Children, the last hour has come. You heard that the antichrist is coming, and in fact many antichrists have already appeared; that is how we know the last hour has come. They went out from among us, but they were never truly part of us. If they had been part of us, they would have remained with us. Their leaving happened so that it would be made plain that none of them are part of us. But as for you, the Holy One has anointed you, and you all know the truth. My reason for writing to you is not that you are ignorant of the truth. It is that you know it, and that nothing false ever comes from the truth. Who is the liar, if not the person who denies that Jesus is the Christ? That person is the antichrist, the one who denies the Father as well as the Son. Anyone who denies the Son is without the Father as well; anyone who confesses the Son has the Father too. You, for your part, must let what you heard from the beginning remain in you. If what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you too will remain in the Son and in the Father. And the promise he himself made to us is this: eternal life.

The anointing that teaches you

I have written these things to you concerning those who are out to deceive you. As for you, you received an anointing from him, and that anointing remains in you; you have no need for anyone to teach you. Rather, his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true and not a lie. So, just as the anointing has taught you, remain in him.

Ready for his coming

And now, dear children, remain in him. Then, when he appears, we will be able to face him boldly at his coming, instead of turning away from him in shame. Since you know that he is righteous, you can be sure that everyone who does what is righteous has been born of him.
fields.summary: Jesus is our advocate with the Father, and whoever knows God keeps God’s commands and walks as Jesus walked. Believers must not love the world, must beware of the antichrists who deny the Son, and remain in what they were taught.

fields.title: 1 John 3
fields.body_html:
Consider the kind of love the Father has given us: we are called children of God, and we really are his children. The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know him. Dear friends, we are children of God now, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. What we do know is this: when he is revealed, we will be like him, for we will see him as he truly is. Everyone whose hope is set on him in this way makes themselves pure, just as he is pure.

Children of God and children of the devil

Everyone who goes on sinning is also practicing lawlessness; sin is lawlessness. You know that he was revealed so that he could take sins away, and he has no sin in him. Whoever remains in him does not go on sinning; whoever goes on sinning has neither seen him nor come to know him. Dear children, do not let anyone mislead you: it is the person who practices righteousness who is righteous, just as he is righteous. Whoever goes on sinning belongs to the devil, because the devil has sinned from the beginning and has never stopped. This is why the Son of God was revealed: to undo the works of the devil. Whoever has been born of God does not go on sinning, for God’s seed remains in them; they are not able to go on sinning, because it is from God that they have been born. This is how it becomes clear who are God’s children and who are the devil’s children: anyone who does not practice righteousness is not from God, and neither is anyone who does not love their brother or sister.

Love one another

For the message you heard from the beginning is this: we should love one another. We must not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil, and his brother’s were righteous. Do not be astonished, brothers and sisters, if the world hates you. We know that we have moved out of death into life, because we love our brothers and sisters. Whoever does not love remains in death. Whoever hates a brother or sister is a murderer, and you know that eternal life does not remain in any murderer. This is how we have come to know what love is: he laid down his life for us. And we in turn owe it to our brothers and sisters to lay down our lives for them. Suppose someone has enough of this world’s goods and notices a brother or sister in need, yet shuts their heart against them. How can the love of God remain in such a person? Dear children, let us love not by what we say or with our tongues, but by what we do and in truth. This is how we will know that we belong to the truth, and how we will set our hearts at rest in his presence whenever our hearts condemn us: God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything. Dear friends, if our hearts do not condemn us, we can approach God boldly, and whatever we ask, we receive from him, since we are keeping his commands and doing what is pleasing in his sight. This is what God commands: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and that we love one another, following the command he gave us. Those who keep his commands remain in God, and God remains in them. We can be sure that he remains in us because of the Spirit he has given us.
fields.summary: God’s great love has made believers children of God, and those who do what is right show it, while the children of the devil go on sinning. Love means laying down one’s life for others, in action and truth.

fields.title: 1 John 4
fields.body_html:
Testing the spirits

Dear friends, do not believe just any spirit; test the spirits to find out whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out and are now in the world. Here is how you recognize the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as one who has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist; you have heard that it is coming, and now it is already in the world. As for you, dear children, you belong to God, and you have already won the victory over them, because the one in you is greater than the one in the world. They belong to the world, so what they say comes from the world, and the world listens to them. We belong to God. Whoever knows God listens to us, and whoever does not belong to God does not listen to us. That is how we tell the Spirit of truth from the spirit of falsehood.

God is love

Dear friends, let us keep loving one another, for love has its source in God; everyone who loves is born of God and knows him. The one who does not love has never known God, for God is love. This is how God’s love was made visible among us: God has sent his one and only Son into the world, so that through him we may have life. This is where love is found: not in our having loved God, but in his loving us and sending his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins. Dear friends, since this is how God loved us, we too should love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has reached completion in us.

Remaining in God

This is how we know that we remain in him and he remains in us: he has given us from his own Spirit. We have seen it with our own eyes, and we testify that the Father has sent the Son as Savior of the world. When anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in them, and they remain in God. We ourselves have come to know the love God has for us, and we believe it.

Love has no room for fear

God is love. Whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in them. In this way love has been brought to completion among us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, for just as he is, so are we in this world. Love has no room for fear; instead, complete love throws fear out, because fear has to do with punishment, and anyone who is afraid has not been brought to completion in love. We love because he loved us first. If someone says, “I love God,” but hates a brother or sister, that person is a liar. For anyone who does not love a brother or sister, whom they have seen, is not able to love God, whom they have not seen. And this is the command we have received from him: the one who loves God is to love a brother or sister as well.
fields.summary: Believers are to test the spirits, for every spirit that confesses Jesus come in the flesh is from God. God is love, shown in sending the Son, and perfect love has no room for fear.

fields.title: 1 John 5
fields.body_html:
Born of God, overcoming the world

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves the child born of him as well. We can tell that we love God’s children when we love God and do what he commands. For to love God is to keep his commandments, and his commandments are no burden, because everything born of God overcomes the world. And our faith is the victory that overcame the world. Who overcomes the world, if not the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is the one who came by water and blood: Jesus Christ. He came not with the water only, but with the water and with the blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth. For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water and the blood, and the three are in agreement. We accept the testimony of people; the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony God has given: he has testified about his Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has this testimony within. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, by refusing to believe the testimony God has given about his Son. And here is what the testimony says: God gave us eternal life, and that life is found in his Son. Anyone who has the Son has the life; anyone without the Son of God does not have the life.

Knowing we have eternal life

I have written these things to you so that you may know that you have eternal life—you who believe in the name of the Son of God. And here is the boldness we have in coming to him: whenever we ask for something in line with his will, he listens to us. And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that the requests we have made of him are ours. If anyone sees their brother or sister committing a sin that does not lead to death, they should ask, and God will give that person life. This is for those whose sin does not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death. I am not saying that anyone should make request about that. All wrongdoing is sin, and yet there is sin that does not lead to death.

What we know

We know that anyone born of God does not go on sinning; rather, the Son, who was born of God, keeps them safe, and the evil one does not lay hold of them. We know that we belong to God, and that the whole world lies in the grip of the evil one. We know too that the Son of God has come and has given us insight to know the one who is true. And we are in the one who is true, since we are in his Son, Jesus Christ. This one is the true God, and eternal life.

Dear children, guard yourselves against idols.
fields.summary: Everyone born of God overcomes the world through faith that Jesus is the Son of God. John writes so that believers may know that they have eternal life, and ends with what they know.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
We know too that the Son of God has come and has given us insight to know the one who is true. And we are in the one who is true, since we are in his Son, Jesus Christ. This one is the true God, and eternal life.

— 1 John 5:20

First John ends where it began, with knowing. The writer has spent five chapters giving anxious believers ways to recognise the truth and to know that they belong to it, and in the last verses the word comes again and again: we know, we know, we know. He has not given them a new teaching. He has taken them back to what they heard “from the beginning”, and shown them that it is enough.

The question the book leaves with you

The letter’s question is not only “Is it true?” but “Do I belong to it?” Every reader of 1 John, sooner or later, lays its tests against their own life. Do I believe that Jesus is the Christ, come in the flesh? Do I keep his commands? Do I love my brothers and sisters, not in words but in deeds?

Those questions can wound, and the writer knows it. That is why he never lets them stand alone. Beside every test he sets the love that came first: “We love because he loved us first” (4:19). The tests are not there to make the reader wonder whether God could ever love them. They are there so that a reader who has been told they are on the outside can see that they are on the inside after all, and stop being afraid.

Where the letter points

It points to Jesus, the one who was heard, seen and touched, who came “by water and blood”, and who stands now as our advocate in the Father’s presence. It points to the church, the small family of “dear children” who must love one another because they are loved. And it points ahead, to a day when God’s children will see him face to face:

Dear friends, we are children of God now, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. What we do know is this: when he is revealed, we will be like him, for we will see him as he truly is.

— 1 John 3:2

Not yet, but surely. That hope, the writer adds, makes a person pure, just as he is pure.

Where to go from here

First John has been loved by the church’s preachers for as long as there has been a church, and many of them are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • Through the whole letter. Augustine of Hippo’s Homilies on the First Epistle of John, ten sermons preached one Easter season, in which he says, “Love, and do what thou wilt.”
  • On light, sin and forgiveness (chapters 1–2). J. C. Ryle’s Are You Forgiven? (2:12) and Thomas Chalmers’s The Expulsive Power of a New Affection (2:15), on why love for the world is driven out only by a greater love.
  • On remaining and on being God’s children (chapters 2–3). A. B. Simpson’s How to Abide (2:28), Andrew Murray’s Abide in Christ, and Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s Adoption (3:1).
  • On God’s love (chapter 4). R. A. Torrey’s The Greatest Sentence That Was Ever Written (4:8) and Charles H. Spurgeon’s Love’s Logic (4:19).
  • On faith that overcomes (chapter 5). Ryle’s Victory (5:4–5).
  • On testing the reality of faith. John Wesley’s A Plain Account of Christian Perfection, which leans on this letter at every turn, and Jonathan Edwards’s A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections, on telling true grace from its counterfeits.
  • From the generation after John. The Epistle and Martyrdom of Polycarp, whose letter to the Philippians repeats this letter’s warning that whoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is antichrist.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to 1 John in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

But the best next step may be to read the Gospel of John beside it, and then to read the letter again. The Gospel tells how the Word became flesh; the letter tells what it means to live in his light. And its last words, so abrupt on a first reading, may come to sound like a father’s blessing at the door:

Dear children, guard yourselves against idols.

— 1 John 5:21
